meta.origin: Hand-curated from the Internal Revenue Code, IRS publications and notices, TreasuryDirect, and the published terms of the plans and issuers named. There is no API for any of this: contribution limits are announced annually in an IRS notice as an HTML page, plan-specific facts live in private plan documents, and state 529 rules live in fifty separate statutes.
meta.note: Approximate figures for the stated date. Every dollar limit here is inflation-indexed and changes each January; income phase-outs move; several of these rules were rewritten by recent legislation. This is not tax advice. Confirm the current numbers on the linked IRS or Treasury page before acting, and take advice before anything irreversible.

fieldNotes.kind: What kind of promise is behind the money: tax_rule and tax_deferral are statutory, employer_promise is one company's plan document, treasury_program is TreasuryDirect, provider_policy is an issuer's own unpublished practice.
fieldNotes.benefit: How the headline rate is computed. 'fixed' is a literal percentage set by statute or plan; 'ordinary', 'ltcg', 'state_only', 'drag', 'muni' and 'state_529' are computed from the user's own tax settings at build time and say so on the row.
fieldNotes.rateOn: What the percentage is a rate ON. Never a portfolio — always the specific money the action moves.
fieldNotes.maxInvestment: The statutory or plan cap on money that earns this rate. The next dollar past it earns nothing, which is why the app blends the rate down over a larger budget.
fieldNotes.window: The deadline, computed from the clock as the NEXT occurrence so a recurring statutory deadline resurfaces every year instead of expiring once.
fieldNotes.appliesTo: Who this is actually available to. Becomes the first requirement on the row, because a benefit described as universal when it is not is a lie by omission.

items.name: Employer 401(k) match — 50% on the first 6% of pay
items.rateOn: every dollar you defer, up to 6% of your pay
items.earlyExitPenalty: 10% early-distribution penalty plus ordinary income tax before 59½
items.appliesTo: employees whose employer offers a matching contribution, which is most but nowhere near all US employers. Nothing here is available to you if your plan does not match.
items.accessNotes: Open your payroll or plan portal and set your deferral percentage to at least the full match threshold — 6% in this formula. That single change is the whole action. Then read the plan's Summary Plan Description for two things: the vesting schedule, and whether the plan trues up at year end.
requirements: You must defer at least 6% of your own pay to collect the whole match — defer 3% and you get half of it
Vesting: employer money commonly vests on a three-year cliff or a six-year graded schedule, and an unvested match is not yours
Leaving before you vest forfeits the unvested employer money entirely, which is the single biggest reason this is not risk-free
The $24,500 cap is on YOUR deferrals for the year, not on the match; the plan may also cap the match separately
Highly compensated employees can have deferrals refunded if the plan fails its annual nondiscrimination testing
items.notes: This is the largest guaranteed return an ordinary person can access, and it is not close. A 50% return, in cash, on the day the money lands, with no market risk on the match itself — nothing else in this app pays anything like it, and no screener will ever show it to you because there is nothing to buy. Not taking the full match is the most expensive routine financial mistake there is.

items.name: Employer 401(k) match — dollar for dollar on the first 3%
items.rateOn: every dollar you defer, up to 3% of your pay
items.appliesTo: employees at a plan using a dollar-for-dollar formula, which is common in smaller and safe-harbor plans.
items.accessNotes: Set your deferral to at least 3% in the payroll portal. If money is genuinely tight this is the one contribution to make before paying down anything short of high-interest debt: a 100% instant return beats every debt rate you are likely to carry.
requirements: You must defer at least 3% of pay yourself — the match is on your money, not a gift
Vesting schedule applies unless the plan is a safe-harbor design, in which case employer contributions vest immediately
A dollar-for-dollar formula usually stops at a low percentage of pay; beyond it the marginal return is zero
items.notes: A 100% return means the money doubles the instant it arrives. Even if the fund you buy inside the plan then falls 30%, you are still up 40% on the year against not contributing at all, which is the arithmetic people miss when they say they are waiting for a better market.

items.name: Safe-harbor basic match — 100% on 3%, then 50% on the next 2%
items.rateOn: the first 5% of pay you defer, blending to 4% of pay from the employer
items.appliesTo: employees at a plan using the statutory safe-harbor basic match, a standard design at small and mid-sized employers.
items.accessNotes: Defer 5% and you collect 4% of pay from the employer. Deferring 4% collects 3.5%, deferring 3% collects 3% — the formula is deliberately front-loaded, so the first dollars are worth more than the last.
requirements: You must defer the full 5% of pay to collect all 4%
Safe-harbor employer contributions are 100% vested immediately, which removes the forfeiture risk that applies to ordinary matches
The blended 80% figure is the whole match divided by the whole 5% deferral; the first 3% is matched at 100% and the next 2% at 50%
items.notes: Worth knowing as a shape rather than a number: matching formulas taper, so the marginal return on your sixth percent of pay is usually zero while the return on your first is 100%. Deferral decisions should be made against the marginal rate, not the average.

items.name: The front-loading trap — match forfeited by hitting the limit early
items.rateOn: the deferrals you would have made in the paychecks after you hit the annual limit
items.appliesTo: high earners who max their 401(k) before December, in a plan that computes the match per pay period and does NOT true up at year end.
items.accessNotes: Find out whether your plan trues up. If it does, front-load freely — you get the whole match regardless of timing. If it does not, work backwards from the annual limit and set a deferral percentage that lands you exactly at the cap with the final paycheck of the year.
requirements: Only bites if you would otherwise hit the annual deferral limit before your last paycheck
Only bites if the plan matches per pay period with no annual true-up — many plans do true up, and for those this is a non-issue
You must fix it by changing your deferral election before the payroll cut-off, which is why the deadline is the calendar year
items.notes: Almost nobody knows this one and it costs thousands. If the match is computed per paycheck and you stop contributing in September because you hit the cap, there is nothing to match in October, November or December, and the employer money for those months is simply gone. Every dollar of match missed this way is a 50% return you declined.

items.name: Timing a job change around the vesting cliff
items.rateOn: whatever employer money is currently unvested in your account
items.uncappedNote: There is no cap on this one because it is not a contribution — it is the employer balance you already have, which becomes yours in full the day you cross the schedule.
items.appliesTo: employees who are considering leaving a job and have employer contributions that have not yet vested. Irrelevant in a safe-harbor plan, where employer money vests immediately.
items.accessNotes: Pull your plan statement and find the vested percentage of the employer portion, then find your vesting date in the Summary Plan Description. If a start date can be moved a few weeks past a cliff, that is often the highest-paid few weeks of your career.
requirements: Federal law caps the schedule at a three-year cliff or six-year graded vesting, but within that the plan chooses
Vesting normally runs on years of SERVICE, not on contribution dates — check whether your plan measures by hours worked or by anniversary
Your own deferrals are always 100% vested; this only ever concerns employer money
Leaving a day before a cliff forfeits the entire unvested amount, and no negotiation recovers it
items.notes: This is the counterweight to every match row here: an unvested match is not your money. Encoded as 100% because that is literally what crossing the line is worth — the unvested balance goes from zero to yours.

items.name: 403(b) and 457(b) together — two full deferral limits in one year
items.rateOn: the second full deferral limit you can shelter, which almost nobody realises is available
items.appliesTo: employees of state and local governments, public schools and some non-profits who are offered BOTH a 403(b) and a governmental 457(b). Not available to private-sector employees, and not available if your employer offers only one of the two.
items.accessNotes: Enrol in both plans through your employer's benefits portal and set a separate deferral election in each. The two limits are genuinely independent — the 457(b) limit is not coordinated with the 403(b) or 401(k) limit, which is unique in the code.
requirements: Requires an employer offering both plan types, which is essentially confined to the public sector and larger non-profits
A 401(k) and a 403(b) DO share one limit — only the 457(b) sits outside it
Non-governmental 457(b) plans (some hospitals and charities) are unsecured claims against the employer's general assets and can be lost in a bankruptcy
Each plan has its own investment menu and its own fees, which can be poor in 403(b) annuity products
items.notes: Teachers, nurses and city employees can shelter roughly double what a private-sector colleague can, and most of them have never been told. The value shown is the deduction on the second limit at your marginal rate.

items.name: Governmental 457(b) — no 10% penalty after you leave
items.rateOn: any money you withdraw before 59½ after separating from service
items.uncappedNote: Not capped as a contribution: this is the penalty you avoid on whatever you withdraw early, so its value scales with how much you take out before 59½.
items.appliesTo: employees with a governmental 457(b) who expect to stop working before 59½. Worth nothing if you will not touch the money until retirement age anyway.
items.accessNotes: Leave the money in the 457(b) when you separate. Rolling it into an IRA feels tidy and permanently destroys this feature — the balance takes on IRA rules, penalty included.
requirements: Governmental 457(b) only; the rule does not extend to 401(k), 403(b) or IRA balances
You must have separated from service — this is not a way to raid the account while still employed
Ordinary income tax still applies in full; only the 10% additional tax is waived
Rolling the balance to an IRA forfeits the exception permanently
items.notes: For anyone planning to retire early this is a genuinely unusual piece of flexibility, and the instinct to consolidate everything into one IRA is exactly what destroys it.

items.name: SIMPLE IRA — the match a small employer is legally required to make
items.rateOn: your deferrals up to 3% of pay, matched dollar for dollar
items.termLabel: Locked until 59½, with a two-year trap on rollovers
items.earlyExitPenalty: 25% penalty on withdrawals in the first two years of participation, not the usual 10%
items.appliesTo: employees of small businesses offering a SIMPLE IRA rather than a 401(k). If your employer sponsors one, the match is not discretionary — it is a condition of the plan.
items.accessNotes: Complete the salary reduction agreement your employer provides and set your deferral to at least 3%. Employer contributions to a SIMPLE are immediately and always 100% vested, so unlike a 401(k) match there is no forfeiture risk.
requirements: The employer must either match up to 3% of pay or contribute 2% of pay for everyone, and the choice is theirs
SIMPLE deferral limits are considerably lower than a 401(k) — roughly $17,000 rather than $24,500
Withdrawals in the first two years of participation carry a 25% penalty rather than 10%, and cannot be rolled to an IRA
Employer contributions vest immediately, which is a genuine advantage over most 401(k) plans
items.notes: The two-year rule is the part that catches people: leaving in year one and rolling the balance to an IRA is a 25% penalty on the whole amount.

items.name: Solo 401(k) — the employer contribution on self-employment income
items.rateOn: the employer-side contribution you make to yourself, roughly 20% of net self-employment income
items.appliesTo: the self-employed and owner-only businesses, including people with a side business alongside a W-2 job. Not available once you have employees other than a spouse.
items.accessNotes: Open a one-participant 401(k) at a large brokerage — most charge nothing to set one up. You wear two hats: you defer as the employee and contribute again as the employer, and the employer side is roughly 20% of net self-employment income after the self-employment tax adjustment.
requirements: No employees other than you and a spouse; hiring one generally ends the plan's eligibility
The employee deferral limit is shared with any 401(k) at your day job — the employer side is not
The plan must be established by the end of the tax year for employee deferrals, though employer contributions can be funded later
Once plan assets pass roughly $250,000 an annual Form 5500-EZ is required
items.notes: Someone with a modest freelance income alongside a salaried job can often shelter the whole side income here. The value shown is the deduction at your marginal rate; the money is taxed as ordinary income on the way out.

items.name: HSA — the only triple-tax-advantaged account there is
items.rateOn: every dollar you contribute, up to roughly $4,400 individual or $8,750 family
items.appliesTo: anyone covered by a qualifying high-deductible health plan and not enrolled in Medicare or claimed as a dependent. If your health plan is not an HDHP you cannot contribute at all, whatever your income.
items.accessNotes: Elect it through your employer at open enrollment, or open one directly at a custodian if you have HDHP coverage outside work. Contribute the maximum, pay current medical costs from cash if you possibly can, and invest the balance rather than leaving it in the cash sweep — most people leave it in cash and lose the whole point.
requirements: Requires HDHP coverage for the months you contribute — deductible and out-of-pocket minimums are set annually by the IRS
Disqualified by any Medicare enrolment, including the six months of retroactive Part A coverage that starts automatically when you claim Social Security after 65
Money spent on non-medical costs before 65 is taxed AND carries a 20% penalty
Those 55 and over can add roughly $1,000 more, but each spouse's catch-up must go into their own account
Family coverage roughly doubles the limit to about $8,750 — the row is priced at the individual cap
items.notes: Deductible going in, growth untaxed, and withdrawals untaxed for qualified medical expenses. No other account does all three, which is why it beats both a 401(k) and a Roth for any dollar you will eventually spend on healthcare — and everyone eventually does.

items.name: Fund the HSA through payroll, not from your bank account
items.rateOn: every dollar routed through payroll instead of contributed directly
items.appliesTo: employees whose employer runs the HSA through a Section 125 cafeteria plan. Self-employed people and anyone contributing directly cannot get this — they get the income tax deduction only.
items.accessNotes: Route the whole contribution through payroll deduction rather than transferring money to the custodian yourself. Same account, same limit, same deduction, plus the payroll tax — it is free and it is purely a matter of which form you fill in.
requirements: The employer must offer HSA contributions through a Section 125 cafeteria plan; not all do
A direct contribution gets the income tax deduction but never recovers the payroll tax — this cannot be fixed at filing time
Above the Social Security wage base only the 1.45% Medicare portion is saved
Reduces reported Social Security wages very slightly, which marginally lowers your eventual benefit
items.notes: An extra 7.65% on the same dollars for choosing one contribution route over another. It is one of the few genuinely free things in the tax code and it exists only through an employer.

items.name: The HSA receipt shoebox — reimburse yourself decades later
items.rateOn: the balance you leave invested instead of spending, compounding entirely untaxed
items.uncappedNote: Not capped, because this is not a contribution: the annual limit applies to what you put in, and this row is about what the whole accumulated balance does once it is in there.
items.appliesTo: HSA holders with enough spare cash to pay medical bills out of pocket now. It is worthless if you need the HSA money to pay this year's bills.
items.accessNotes: Pay qualified medical expenses from ordinary cash, keep every receipt and an itemised log, and leave the HSA invested. There is no deadline to reimburse yourself: a receipt from 2026 can be reimbursed tax-free in 2056, so the account becomes an unlimited-horizon, entirely tax-free investment account with a personal liquidity option attached.
requirements: The expense must have been incurred after the HSA was established — earlier bills never qualify
You must actually keep the records; with no receipt there is no tax-free reimbursement, and the burden of proof is yours
Expenses reimbursed by insurance or already deducted on a return cannot be used again
Most custodians charge fees or impose a cash minimum before they let you invest, which is a separate row here
items.notes: This is the play that turns the HSA into the best account in the code. The rate shown is the annual tax drag you avoid at an assumed 6% return, which understates it badly over decades — the real prize is that qualified withdrawals are never taxed at all.

items.name: Move the HSA to a custodian that does not charge you
items.rateOn: the whole HSA balance, every year, as fees you stop paying
items.uncappedNote: Uncapped: a percentage fee is charged on the whole balance, so the bigger the account the more this is worth in dollars.
items.appliesTo: anyone whose employer-chosen HSA custodian charges a monthly administration fee, an investment fee, or requires a large cash balance before investing. Many do; a few charge nothing.
items.accessNotes: Keep contributing through payroll to capture the payroll tax, then periodically transfer the balance to a no-fee custodian by trustee-to-trustee transfer. That transfer is unlimited and does not count against the once-per-year rollover rule.
requirements: Use a trustee-to-trustee transfer, not a rollover: rollovers are limited to one per twelve months and a missed 60-day deadline is taxable
Some employers only make their contribution to the in-house custodian, so the account usually has to stay open
Check for an account-closing fee before moving
A cash-balance requirement before investing is itself a cost — idle cash in an HSA earns almost nothing
items.notes: A 0.4% annual fee on a balance meant to compound for thirty years is roughly a tenth of the ending balance. This is the least exciting row here and it is close to free money.

items.name: Traditional IRA deduction — and the April deadline nobody uses
items.rateOn: every deductible dollar you contribute, up to roughly $7,500
items.appliesTo: people with earned income who are either not covered by a workplace retirement plan, or are covered and fall under the income phase-out. Above the phase-out with a workplace plan, the contribution is allowed but NOT deductible, and this row is worth nothing to you.
items.accessNotes: Open an IRA anywhere, contribute, and tell the custodian which tax year the contribution is for — this is the step people get wrong. Until the April filing deadline both the prior year and the current year are open at once, so a contribution made in March can be a deduction on the return you are filing that week.
requirements: Requires earned income at least equal to the contribution
Deductibility phases out at modest income if you or a spouse are covered by a workplace plan; without workplace coverage there is no income limit
The IRA limit is shared with any Roth IRA contribution for the same year — it is one limit between the two
The prior-year window closes at the April filing deadline with no extension, even if you extend the return itself
items.notes: The dual-year window is the most under-used deadline in the code. In the first fifteen weeks of a year you can still change last year's tax bill, which is not true of almost anything else here.

items.name: Roth IRA — no deduction, and never taxed again
items.rateOn: the balance you shelter, as tax you never pay on its growth
items.appliesTo: people with earned income below the Roth phase-out — roughly $150,000 to $165,000 single and $240,000 to $250,000 married filing jointly, indexed annually. Above it you cannot contribute directly, and the backdoor row is the route instead.
items.accessNotes: Contribute anywhere, specify the tax year, and invest it — an uninvested Roth is the most common way people waste this. Your own contributions (not the earnings) can be withdrawn at any age with no tax and no penalty, which quietly makes a Roth a usable emergency fund as well as a retirement account.
requirements: Requires earned income, and the contribution phases out at higher incomes
The limit is shared with a traditional IRA — roughly $7,500 in total across both
Earnings come out tax-free only after 59½ and five years from your first Roth contribution
Contributions can be withdrawn at any time without tax or penalty; earnings cannot
items.notes: The value shown is the annual tax drag you avoid on an assumed 7% return, which is the honest way to price a shelter: it is worth your tax rate times whatever the account actually earns, and nothing at all if it earns nothing.

items.name: Backdoor Roth — the route above the income limit
items.rateOn: the balance you get into a Roth that you were not allowed to contribute to directly
items.appliesTo: people whose income is ABOVE the Roth contribution phase-out. Below it this is pointless — you simply contribute to a Roth directly, and doing the backdoor version instead adds paperwork for no benefit. It is also unusable, in practice, if you hold any pre-tax IRA money.
items.accessNotes: Make a non-deductible contribution to a traditional IRA, then convert it to a Roth shortly afterwards, and file Form 8606 for both steps. The conversion is only tax-free because the contribution was after-tax and there was nothing to grow in between.
requirements: Only useful above the Roth income phase-out — below it, contribute directly instead
The pro-rata rule is the trap: if you hold ANY pre-tax money in any traditional, SEP or SIMPLE IRA on 31 December, the conversion is taxed proportionally across all of them
The usual fix is rolling existing pre-tax IRA money into a 401(k) first, which requires a plan that accepts roll-ins
Form 8606 must be filed for the non-deductible contribution or you will be taxed twice on the same money
This is a widely used technique with no explicit statutory blessing, and legislation to close it has been proposed repeatedly
items.notes: Describing this as available to everyone would be simply wrong in both directions: it is useless below the phase-out and often unusable above it if you have a rollover IRA sitting there. Check the pro-rata position before the first step, not after.

items.name: Mega-backdoor Roth — after-tax 401(k) money converted in-plan
items.rateOn: the very large balance this can move into a Roth in a single year
items.appliesTo: employees whose plan allows BOTH after-tax (not Roth) contributions and either in-plan Roth conversion or in-service withdrawals. Most plans allow neither, and no amount of income makes this available if the plan document does not permit it.
items.accessNotes: Call the plan administrator and ask two specific questions: does the plan accept after-tax contributions beyond the elective deferral limit, and does it allow in-plan Roth conversions or in-service distributions. If both answers are yes, contribute after-tax up to the overall limit and convert immediately so nothing accrues taxable earnings.
requirements: Requires an explicitly permissive plan document — this is the binding constraint, not your income
The room is the overall annual addition limit (about $72,000) minus your own deferrals minus all employer contributions, so a generous match shrinks it
Convert promptly: any earnings on the after-tax money before conversion are taxable
Plans that permit after-tax contributions can still fail nondiscrimination testing and refund them
items.notes: The largest Roth shelter available to an employee, and probably the least known. The cap shown assumes a full deferral and no employer contribution; work out your own room from your plan's numbers.

items.name: HSA contributions for last year, made in the spring
items.rateOn: a prior-year HSA contribution made after the calendar year has already closed
items.appliesTo: anyone who had qualifying HDHP coverage last year and did not use the whole HSA limit. If you were not HDHP-covered last year there is nothing to claim.
items.accessNotes: Contribute directly to the custodian and mark it as a prior-year contribution — the custodian's web form has a tax-year selector and defaults to the current year, which is how people lose this by accident. It is deductible on the return you are about to file.
requirements: You must have been HSA-eligible for the months you are contributing for; the limit is prorated by eligible month
The window closes at the April filing deadline, with no extension
A direct contribution recovers income tax only, never the payroll tax you would have saved through payroll last year
The last-month rule, which lets December coverage buy a full-year contribution, imposes a thirteen-month testing period with a penalty if you break it
items.notes: Almost everyone knows the IRA version of this deadline and almost nobody knows the HSA one, even though the HSA deduction is worth more per dollar.

items.name: Convert to Roth in a low-income year
items.rateOn: every dollar you convert while your income is temporarily low
items.uncappedNote: There is no limit on how much you can convert. The practical cap is the top of the bracket you are willing to fill, because a conversion that pushes you into the next bracket is taxed there.
items.appliesTo: people with pre-tax retirement money who are having an unusually low-income year — a sabbatical, a redundancy, a business loss, or the gap between retiring and claiming Social Security. It is worth nothing, and possibly negative, in a normal earning year.
items.accessNotes: Convert only as much as fills the bracket you are content to pay, and stop there. Compute it in December when the year's income is actually known, not in January when it is a guess. Pay the tax from outside the account if you possibly can, so the whole converted balance keeps compounding.
requirements: There is no income limit and no dollar limit on a conversion — only on contributions
Conversions cannot be undone; recharacterisation of conversions was repealed in 2018
Each conversion starts its own five-year clock before the converted amount can be withdrawn penalty-free before 59½
A conversion raises adjusted gross income, which can raise ACA premium credits clawbacks, Medicare IRMAA surcharges two years later, and the taxable share of Social Security
items.notes: The value shown is the gap between your current federal bracket and an assumed 12% in the low year. Both numbers are yours to check — the whole play is arbitrage between two of your own tax years.

items.name: Saver's Credit — a credit, not a deduction, for lower incomes
items.rateOn: the first $2,000 you contribute to any retirement account, at the top 50% tier
items.appliesTo: lower-income savers only. The 50% tier requires adjusted gross income of roughly $24,000 or less filing single and $48,000 or less married filing jointly; above that it steps to 20% and then 10%, and it disappears entirely at roughly $40,000 single or $80,000 joint. Anyone above those figures gets nothing.
items.accessNotes: Contribute to any 401(k), IRA or ABLE account, then file Form 8880 with your return. It is a credit against tax owed, not a deduction from income, so at the top tier a $2,000 contribution cuts your tax bill by $1,000 — on top of any deduction the contribution itself earns.
requirements: Strict AGI limits, and the tiers are cliffs: a dollar of extra income can cut the credit from 50% to 20%
Non-refundable — it can reduce your tax to zero but never generates a refund beyond that, which is why many eligible people get nothing from it
You must be 18 or over, not a full-time student and not claimed as a dependent
Recent distributions from retirement accounts reduce the contribution the credit is computed on
items.notes: This is a 50% return, from the federal government, for people who can least afford to save — and it is among the most under-claimed provisions in the code, largely because it is non-refundable and so invisible to anyone who owes no tax.

items.name: Saver's Match — the credit becomes cash in the account
items.rateOn: the first $2,000 you contribute, paid as a federal deposit into the account rather than as a credit
items.appliesTo: lower and middle income savers, from tax years beginning after 2026. The income phase-out is higher than the old credit's, so some people who never qualified for the Saver's Credit will qualify for this.
items.accessNotes: Nothing to do yet. The point of knowing now is to have an eligible account open and a contribution habit running when it starts, because the match is paid into a retirement account and you need one to receive it.
requirements: Effective for tax years beginning after 31 December 2026 under the SECURE 2.0 Act — it does not exist before then
Paid as a government contribution INTO your retirement account, not as a refund you can spend
Phases out with income, and the implementing regulations were still being written at the snapshot date
It replaces the Saver's Credit rather than stacking with it
items.notes: A legislated, dated, upcoming opportunity. The difference from the old credit matters: a non-refundable credit is worthless to someone who owes no tax, and a deposit is not.

items.name: Tax-loss harvesting — $3,000 against ordinary income
items.rateOn: the $3,000 of realised net loss you can deduct from ordinary income each year
items.appliesTo: anyone holding a losing position in a TAXABLE account. Losses inside an IRA or 401(k) are worth nothing at all — there is nothing to deduct them from.
items.accessNotes: Sell the losing position before the last trading day of the year, and immediately buy something similar but not substantially identical so you stay invested — a different index fund tracking a different index is the standard move. The loss nets against gains first; up to $3,000 of what is left comes off ordinary income, and the rest carries forward forever.
requirements: The loss must be REALISED — an unsold loser is worth nothing, and the sale must settle within the calendar year
Wash-sale rule: buying the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days BEFORE or AFTER the sale disallows the loss
The wash-sale window spans all your accounts, including your IRA and your spouse's — and a repurchase inside an IRA destroys the loss permanently rather than deferring it
Automatic dividend reinvestment is the most common accidental wash sale
The $3,000 ordinary-income cap is per year, not per position, and has not been indexed since 1978
items.notes: At a 24% federal bracket that $3,000 is $720 in cash, every year until the carryforward runs out — the percentage above is computed for your own bracket and state, so read that one. It is one of very few deadlines in this app that is genuinely hard: 31 December, no extensions, and it is exactly when everybody forgets.

items.name: Harvest losses to erase realised gains — no cap at all
items.rateOn: every dollar of realised capital gain you cancel out with a realised loss
items.uncappedNote: Uncapped: losses offset gains dollar for dollar without limit. Only the leftover that comes off ordinary income is capped at $3,000, and that is the separate row.
items.appliesTo: anyone who has realised capital gains this year and also holds losing positions in a taxable account. If you have no gains to offset, the $3,000 ordinary-income row is the one that applies to you.
items.accessNotes: Before the year ends, total your realised gains, then sell enough losers to cancel them. Short-term losses offset short-term gains first, which is the more valuable pairing because short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income. Rebalancing a drifted portfolio is usually free while you have a loss bank to absorb the gains.
requirements: The wash-sale rule applies exactly as it does to any other harvest, across all your accounts and your spouse's
Losses offset the same character of gain first — short against short, long against long — before crossing over
Unused losses carry forward indefinitely but cannot be carried back by an individual
Harvesting resets your cost basis lower, so it defers tax rather than erasing it unless the position is eventually stepped up at death or given away
items.notes: The rate shown is your long-term capital gains rate plus state, because that is what the offset saves. Against short-term gains it is worth considerably more — your full ordinary rate.

items.name: Harvesting digital-asset losses without the 30-day wait
items.rateOn: the loss you realise and deduct, up to the same $3,000 ordinary-income cap
items.appliesTo: holders of digital assets at a loss in a taxable account. Not applicable to crypto held inside a retirement account, and not applicable to tokenised securities, which are securities.
items.accessNotes: Sell at a loss and, on the current reading of the law, buy back immediately — the position is unchanged and the loss is banked. Keep the trade records: exchange reporting has improved but the basis tracking is still largely your problem.
requirements: The wash-sale rule in section 1091 applies to stocks and securities; the IRS treats digital assets as property, so on the current reading it does not reach them
Legislation to extend the wash-sale rule to digital assets has been proposed in nearly every budget cycle and could pass at any time — verify the position for the year you are acting in
Economic substance and step-transaction doctrines still apply; a sale that is not a real sale is not a real loss
The $3,000 ordinary-income cap and the carryforward work exactly as they do for shares
items.notes: Flagged as uncertain deliberately. The technique is widely used and rests on a distinction that Congress has repeatedly tried to remove, so it is one of the few rows here whose legal basis could change between now and December.

items.name: Donate appreciated shares instead of cash
items.provider: Any public charity or donor-advised fund
items.rateOn: the unrealised gain in the shares you donate, which is never taxed to anyone
items.uncappedNote: Not capped in dollars, but the deduction for appreciated property is limited to 30% of adjusted gross income in a year, with a five-year carryforward of the excess.
items.appliesTo: people who already intend to give to charity, itemise their deductions, and hold appreciated shares held more than a year in a taxable account. If you take the standard deduction, only the avoided capital gain is worth anything to you.
items.accessNotes: Transfer the shares in kind to the charity or to a donor-advised fund rather than selling them first. The charity sells free of tax, you deduct the full market value if you itemise, and the embedded gain simply disappears. Give the shares with the largest gain and the longest holding period.
requirements: Shares must be held more than one year — short-term holdings are deductible only at cost basis
The gain avoided is worth something whether or not you itemise; the deduction is worth something only if you do
Deduction for appreciated property is capped at 30% of AGI with a five-year carryforward
The charity must be a qualifying public charity, and gifts over $5,000 of non-publicly-traded property need an appraisal
Donating a LOSING position is backwards — sell it, harvest the loss, and donate the cash
items.notes: The rate shown is your long-term capital gains rate plus state, which is the tax on the gain that nobody ever pays. Any deduction you also get from itemising sits on top of that.

items.name: Qualified charitable distribution straight from an IRA
items.rateOn: the amount you send directly from the IRA to charity, which never enters your income at all
items.appliesTo: IRA owners aged 70½ or older who give to charity. Not available before 70½, not available from a 401(k), and worth nothing to someone who does not give anyway.
items.accessNotes: Instruct the IRA custodian to send the money directly to the charity — it must never touch your bank account. It counts towards your required minimum distribution and is excluded from income entirely, which beats a deduction because it lowers adjusted gross income rather than taxable income.
requirements: You must be 70½ or older on the date of the distribution — the age for required distributions is later, and this one is not
IRAs only; a 401(k) must be rolled to an IRA first
Annual limit of roughly $108,000 per person, indexed each year
The money must go directly from custodian to charity; a cheque paid to you first disqualifies it
Donor-advised funds and private foundations do not qualify
items.notes: Excluding income beats deducting it. Lower adjusted gross income also means less of your Social Security is taxable and a lower chance of a Medicare IRMAA surcharge two years later, neither of which a plain charitable deduction achieves.

items.name: Harvest gains at the 0% capital gains rate
items.rateOn: the long-term gains you deliberately realise while your taxable income is low enough to be taxed at zero
items.uncappedNote: Capped by the bracket, not by a dollar limit: gains are free until your taxable income reaches roughly $48,000 single or $97,000 married filing jointly, then taxed at 15% above that.
items.appliesTo: people whose taxable income falls in the 0% long-term capital gains band — early retirees before Social Security starts, students, people between jobs, and low-earning years generally. It is worth nothing in a normal high-earning year.
items.accessNotes: Sell appreciated long-term holdings up to the top of the 0% band and immediately buy them back. There is no wash-sale rule on GAINS, only on losses, so the position is unchanged and your cost basis is permanently reset higher, at no tax cost whatsoever.
requirements: Only long-term gains qualify — the holding must be more than a year
The band is measured on taxable income after deductions, and the gains themselves count towards filling it
Overshooting the top of the band taxes only the excess, not the whole amount
Realised gains raise adjusted gross income and can cut ACA premium credits, which frequently costs more than the tax saved
State tax may still apply even when the federal rate is zero
items.notes: The mirror image of loss harvesting and far less known. Every dollar of basis you step up for free is a dollar of gain you never pay on later.

items.name: Net unrealised appreciation on company stock in a 401(k)
items.rateOn: the appreciation in employer stock held inside the plan, taxed as capital gain instead of ordinary income
items.uncappedNote: Uncapped, and its value scales with how much the stock has appreciated: the play is worth nothing on stock with little gain and a great deal on decades of it.
items.appliesTo: long-tenured employees holding highly appreciated EMPLOYER stock inside a 401(k) or ESOP, at a distributable event. Irrelevant to anyone holding only funds, which is nearly everyone.
items.accessNotes: At a qualifying distribution, move the employer shares in kind to a taxable brokerage account and roll everything else to an IRA. You pay ordinary income tax on the original cost basis only; the appreciation is taxed at long-term capital gains rates whenever you eventually sell, even if you sell the next day.
requirements: Requires a lump-sum distribution of the entire plan balance in one tax year following a triggering event — separation, 59½, death or disability
The shares must move in kind to a taxable account; rolling them into an IRA destroys the election permanently
You owe ordinary income tax on the cost basis in the year of distribution, in cash, up front
Before 55 the 10% early-distribution penalty can apply to that basis
Concentrated single-stock risk is the real cost, and it is not a tax question
items.notes: The value shown is the gap between your ordinary rate and your long-term capital gains rate, which is what the election converts. For someone with thirty years of company stock this is one of the largest single tax decisions of their life, and it is irreversible.

items.name: The rule of 55 — penalty-free 401(k) access after leaving at 55
items.rateOn: whatever you withdraw from that plan between 55 and 59½
items.uncappedNote: Not a contribution and so not capped: this is the 10% penalty you avoid on whatever you withdraw, so it is worth 10% of however much you take.
items.appliesTo: people who separate from an employer in or after the calendar year they turn 55, and still have money in THAT employer's plan. It does not apply to IRAs, and it does not apply to plans from previous employers.
items.accessNotes: Leave the money in the departing employer's 401(k) rather than rolling it to an IRA. Rolling it feels like housekeeping and immediately converts the balance to IRA rules, where withdrawals before 59½ carry the 10% penalty.
requirements: Separation must occur in or after the year you turn 55 — leaving at 54 and waiting does not qualify
Applies only to the plan of the employer you just left, not to older 401(k)s or any IRA
The plan must permit partial withdrawals; some force a lump sum, which makes the exception useless in practice
Ordinary income tax still applies to everything you withdraw
Age 50 rather than 55 for qualified public safety employees
items.notes: Consolidating old accounts into one IRA is standard advice and, for someone leaving work in their mid-fifties, it can be an expensive habit.

items.name: Qualified small business stock — gain excluded under section 1202
items.rateOn: the gain on qualifying shares, up to the greater of $10 million or ten times your basis
items.appliesTo: founders and early employees who acquired stock directly from a qualifying domestic C corporation with under $50 million of gross assets at issuance. It is unavailable on shares bought on the secondary market, on LLC or S-corporation interests, and to almost everyone.
items.accessNotes: This is decided years before it pays: get the company's QSBS status confirmed in writing at issuance, hold the shares at least five years, and keep the documentation. Exercising options early can start the clock sooner, at the cost of paying for the shares.
requirements: Original issuance from a qualifying domestic C corporation only — not purchased shares, not partnerships, not S corporations
Five-year holding period, which recent legislation has begun to tier for partial exclusions at three and four years
Excluded businesses are broad: professional services, financial services, hospitality, farming and mining among them
State treatment varies and several states, California included, do not follow the federal exclusion at all
The rules were amended in 2025 and the asset and exclusion thresholds differ by issuance date — the vintage of your shares decides which version applies
items.notes: Potentially the largest single tax exclusion available to an individual. Priced here at your long-term capital gains rate plus state, because that is what the exclusion saves per dollar of gain; whether you have any qualifying gain at all is entirely a question of how you acquired the shares.

items.name: Pay the safe harbor, not a penny more, and keep the carry
items.rateOn: the tax you would have prepaid early, left in Treasury bills until it is actually due
items.uncappedNote: Uncapped, and worth the short-term rate on whatever you would otherwise have handed over months ahead of the deadline.
items.appliesTo: people with income that is not withheld — the self-employed, investors with large realised gains, anyone with a windfall. Salaried employees with accurate withholding have nothing to gain here.
items.accessNotes: Pay estimated tax to hit the safe harbor exactly — generally 100% of last year's tax, or 110% if your income was high — and keep the rest earning until the filing deadline. Separately: withholding is treated as paid evenly across the year no matter when it happens, so a large fourth-quarter withholding can cure an underpayment from March, which an estimated payment in December cannot.
requirements: The safe harbor is based on LAST year's tax, so it only works if you know that figure
Miss the safe harbor and the underpayment penalty is charged at the federal short-term rate plus three points, compounded daily
Estimated payments are credited when made; withholding is deemed spread evenly across the year, which is the whole trick
State estimated tax rules are separate and frequently stricter
items.notes: Priced at roughly the short-term Treasury yield at the snapshot date, because that is what the money earns while you keep it: this is a carry trade against your own tax bill, not a tax saving. The withholding-timing point is the genuinely obscure part and is worth considerably more than the carry in a year with a late windfall.

items.name: Series I bonds — buying before the rate reset
items.rateOn: the bond you buy, locked at the current composite for a full six months from purchase
items.earlyExitPenalty: Three months of interest if redeemed before five years; cannot be redeemed at all in the first twelve months
items.appliesTo: anyone with a Social Security number and a bank account. This is one of the few rows here with no eligibility test at all.
items.accessNotes: Open a TreasuryDirect account — the process is clunky and can require a signature guarantee, so start it well before a deadline you care about. The composite rate is fixed for six months from your purchase MONTH, not from the calendar year, so a purchase made days before a reset locks the old rate for six months and only then moves to the new one.
requirements: Rates reset on 1 May and 1 November; each bond keeps the rate in force at purchase for its first six months
$10,000 per person per calendar year through TreasuryDirect; paper bonds via tax refund were discontinued
Cannot be redeemed at all in the first twelve months
Redeeming before five years forfeits the last three months of interest
The composite rate is a fixed rate plus twice the semiannual CPI change, so the inflation half can go to zero — but the composite is floored at zero and never negative
items.notes: The series shown is the published composite rate history, not a price — it is there to show how far and how fast this moves. The 4% figure is approximate at the snapshot date and will be wrong by the time you read it: check the current composite on TreasuryDirect before buying.

items.name: The I-bond annual allowance resets on 1 January
items.rateOn: the $10,000 per person allowance that expires unused at the end of every calendar year
items.appliesTo: anyone wanting more than $10,000 of I bonds. The limit is per person per calendar year and it does not carry forward.
items.accessNotes: The limit is per Social Security number, so a couple can buy $20,000 a year, and each child with their own number is another $10,000 held in a custodial-style linked account. A trust or a business entity with its own taxpayer identification number gets its own separate $10,000 allowance, which is how larger positions are legitimately built.
requirements: $10,000 per person per calendar year, and an unused year is gone permanently
Entity accounts (trusts, LLCs, sole proprietorships with an EIN) have their own limits, but entity accounts on TreasuryDirect are administratively painful
Gift-box purchases can be bought now and delivered in a later year, but they count against the RECIPIENT's limit in the year of delivery
Buying on 31 December and again on 1 January uses two years' allowances two days apart
items.notes: A use-it-or-lose-it allowance, which is why the deadline matters more than the rate. The rate shown is the approximate composite at the snapshot date.

items.name: The fifteen-month I-bond hold
items.rateOn: the bond, after deliberately forfeiting the three lowest-rate months on the way out
items.earlyExitPenalty: Three months of interest, which this strategy chooses to pay
items.appliesTo: I-bond holders who want the money back rather than a thirty-year position, and who are watching the rate fall. It is the wrong move when the next composite is higher than the last.
items.accessNotes: Hold for fifteen months and redeem. You have earned fifteen months of interest and forfeit the last three, so you keep twelve months of interest for fifteen months of committed money — and because you choose the exit, the three months you give up are the three at the newest, lowest rate.
requirements: Only sensible when the current composite is below the one you locked in — otherwise hold
The twelve-month minimum hold still applies, so fifteen months is the shortest sensible round trip
The forfeited three months are the most recent three, which is what makes the timing work
Federal tax on all the accrued interest is due in the year you redeem
items.notes: The effective rate shown is the composite scaled by twelve months of interest over fifteen months of commitment. It is the standard way experienced holders exit, and it is written nowhere on TreasuryDirect.

items.name: Series EE bonds — guaranteed to double at twenty years
items.rateOn: the purchase price, as a guaranteed compound rate if and only if you hold exactly twenty years
items.earlyExitPenalty: Redeeming before twenty years pays only the stated rate, which is currently a small fraction of this
items.appliesTo: anyone able to commit money for a full twenty years and wanting a government-guaranteed floor. Anyone who might need the money sooner should not touch these — redeemed early they pay the stated rate, which is close to nothing.
items.accessNotes: Buy through TreasuryDirect. Treasury guarantees the bond will be worth at least twice its purchase price at twenty years, making a one-off adjustment at that date if the stated rate has not got there. That guarantee works out to about 3.53% compounded — a rate you cannot lose, from the US government, for two decades.
requirements: The guarantee applies at exactly twenty years; redeeming at nineteen forfeits nearly all of it
The stated rate on new EE bonds is far below 3.53%, so essentially the entire return comes from the doubling adjustment
$10,000 per person per calendar year, separate from the I-bond limit
Cannot be redeemed in the first twelve months, and forfeits three months of interest before five years
Interest is federally taxable at redemption and never taxed by a state
items.notes: One of the few genuinely contractual twenty-year guarantees available to a retail buyer at any size, and almost nobody knows it exists. It is only a good deal if you truly hold all twenty years.

items.name: Savings bond interest excluded when spent on tuition
items.rateOn: the accrued interest you redeem in a year you pay qualified higher-education expenses
items.uncappedNote: Uncapped in dollars, but phased out entirely at moderate incomes and limited to the amount of qualified expenses you actually paid that year.
items.appliesTo: people who bought EE or I bonds in their OWN name at age 24 or older, and later pay qualified higher-education expenses. Bonds registered to the child do not qualify, which disqualifies most of the people who bought them for exactly this purpose.
items.accessNotes: Redeem the bonds in the same calendar year you pay tuition, and file Form 8815. Paying the expenses into a 529 plan also counts as a qualified expense, which is the flexible route when the tuition bill and the redemption year do not line up.
requirements: The bond owner must have been at least 24 years old on the first day of the month the bond was issued
The bond must be registered to you or you and a spouse, never to the student as owner
Married taxpayers must file jointly to claim it at all
The exclusion phases out at moderate income and disappears entirely above it, and the thresholds are indexed
Only tuition and fees qualify — room, board and books do not
items.notes: The registration requirement is the one that catches people, years after the bonds were bought and long past any chance of fixing it. Worth checking before you buy, not before you redeem.

items.name: Treasury interest is exempt from state income tax
items.rateOn: the yield on Treasury bills and notes, as state tax you never pay on it
items.uncappedNote: Uncapped: the exemption applies to every dollar of Treasury interest you receive, at any size.
items.appliesTo: residents of states that tax income. In a state with no income tax this is worth exactly nothing, and it is shown at zero rather than hidden, because knowing not to pay up for it matters as much as knowing to chase it.
items.accessNotes: Hold Treasuries directly or in a Treasury-only fund and the interest escapes state and local income tax by federal statute. Money-market funds report the government share each year, and a fund that mixes in repurchase agreements loses the exemption on that slice in several states — California, New York and Connecticut require a 50% government-obligation threshold before any of it passes through.
requirements: Federal income tax still applies in full; only state and local tax is barred
Capital gains on a Treasury sold before maturity are not interest and are taxable by the state
Fund distributions only pass the exemption through to the extent of actual government interest, and some states impose a minimum threshold
Treasury repurchase agreements are generally NOT exempt, which quietly disqualifies part of many money-market funds
items.notes: This is why a Treasury at a lower headline rate frequently beats a savings account at a higher one — for a high-tax-state resident the comparison flips at a spread of a quarter point or more. The app's after-tax ranking already applies this to every Treasury row; this row is the rule itself and what it is worth to you.

items.name: Municipal bond interest — federally exempt, and in-state doubly so
items.rateOn: municipal interest, as federal and in-state tax you never pay on it
items.uncappedNote: Uncapped, and worth more the higher your bracket — which is precisely why munis are priced for high earners and are usually a poor deal for everyone else.
items.appliesTo: taxable-account investors in higher federal brackets, and especially residents of high-tax states buying their own state's paper. In a low bracket the exemption is worth less than the yield you give up, and in a retirement account it is worth nothing at all.
items.accessNotes: Buy a fund of your own state's bonds for the double exemption, or a national fund if your state does not tax or does not offer one. Compare on tax-equivalent yield, never on the headline: this app computes that for every municipal row already.
requirements: Never hold munis in an IRA or 401(k) — you would be paying for an exemption you already have
Private activity bonds can be taxable under the alternative minimum tax
Capital gains on a muni are fully taxable; only the interest is exempt
In-state funds are concentrated in one issuer's credit, which is real risk in exchange for the state exemption
A handful of states tax their own municipal interest, and several exempt all states' — check yours
items.notes: Computed for your state as if you hold in-state paper. If you hold out-of-state municipals, the state slice does not apply and the benefit is the federal exemption alone.

items.name: 529 contributions — the state deduction, which varies enormously
items.rateOn: the contribution your state lets you deduct, returned immediately as a lower state tax bill
items.uncappedNote: No cap applies for you: either your state deducts the whole contribution, or it offers nothing at all and there is nothing to cap. The row above says which.
items.earlyExitPenalty: 10% federal penalty on the earnings portion of a non-qualified withdrawal, plus income tax and often state recapture of the deduction
items.appliesTo: residents of states offering a 529 deduction or credit, which is most but not all of them. Nine states have no income tax and a handful more — California and North Carolina among them — tax income and give nothing for 529 contributions.
items.accessNotes: Contribute to your own state's plan before 31 December and claim the deduction on the state return. In a parity state the deduction follows contributions to ANY state's plan, so you can take your home deduction while holding a cheaper plan elsewhere. Several states allow contributions right up to the April filing deadline instead — the rest are strictly calendar-year.
requirements: The benefit is a STATE benefit; there is no federal deduction for 529 contributions
Caps vary from unlimited to $500 a year, and several are per beneficiary rather than per taxpayer, which multiplies for larger families
Most states only allow the deduction on their own plan, so it has to be weighed against that plan's fees
Many states recapture the deduction if you later take a non-qualified withdrawal or roll to another state's plan
A deduction is worth your state rate; a credit is worth its stated percentage whatever your bracket
items.notes: Computed from the state in your tax settings against a table of approximate state rules. State 529 caps change most years — confirm yours before contributing, especially if the cap is what you are contributing up to.

items.name: Roll leftover 529 money into the beneficiary's Roth IRA
items.rateOn: the leftover balance you move to a Roth instead of withdrawing it non-qualified
items.appliesTo: families with money left in a 529 after education is finished, where the account has existed for at least fifteen years and the beneficiary has earned income. Not available on a recently opened account.
items.accessNotes: Do it as a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into a Roth IRA in the BENEFICIARY's name. It is limited to the annual IRA contribution limit each year, so a full $35,000 takes several years, and it uses up the beneficiary's own IRA room for those years.
requirements: The 529 account must have been open at least fifteen years, and changing the beneficiary may restart that clock
Contributions made in the last five years, and their earnings, are not eligible to move
The beneficiary must have earned income at least equal to the amount rolled in each year
Lifetime cap of $35,000 per beneficiary, and each year's rollover counts against that year's IRA limit
Several states have not conformed and may treat the rollover as a non-qualified withdrawal for state tax purposes
items.notes: Priced at the 10% penalty this avoids; you also avoid ordinary income tax on the earnings portion, so the real saving is materially larger. It removes the main objection to funding a 529 heavily — that the money is trapped if the child does not need it.

items.name: Superfund a 529 with five years of gifts at once
items.rateOn: the whole balance, compounding untaxed for years longer than it otherwise would have
items.appliesTo: people with enough capital to front-load a child's education fund and a reason to move money out of a taxable estate. Irrelevant to anyone contributing monthly out of income.
items.accessNotes: Contribute up to five years of the annual gift-tax exclusion in one go — roughly $95,000 per donor per beneficiary, or double from a couple — and elect on Form 709 to spread it over five years for gift-tax purposes. The money starts compounding tax-free immediately instead of arriving in annual instalments.
requirements: Requires a Form 709 gift-tax return electing the five-year spread, even though no gift tax is usually due
No further gifts to that beneficiary for five years without eating into your lifetime exemption
Dying within the five years pulls a proportional part back into the estate
A state deduction is usually still capped at its normal annual figure, so superfunding does not multiply it
The gift is irrevocable — this is a gift, and you cannot take it back
items.notes: The value shown is the annual tax drag avoided on an assumed 6% return; the real benefit is the extra years of compounding, which a single-year rate understates badly.

items.name: Health FSA — pre-tax, and gone at year end
items.rateOn: every dollar you elect, which never appears as taxable wages at all
items.appliesTo: employees whose employer offers a health FSA. Not available to the self-employed, and not compatible with contributing to an HSA except in the limited-purpose form.
items.accessNotes: Elect an amount at open enrollment that you are confident you will spend — the whole election is available on day one, even before you have contributed it, which is a genuine and under-appreciated feature. Then spend it: this is the one benefit here with a real use-it-or-lose-it rule.
requirements: Use-it-or-lose-it: unspent money is forfeited to the employer at year end, subject to a carryover of roughly $680 or a grace period if the plan offers one
The election is fixed for the year and can only be changed on a qualifying life event
Cannot be combined with HSA contributions unless the FSA is limited to dental and vision
The full annual election is available from day one and is not clawed back if you leave mid-year having overspent it
Saves income tax and payroll tax, which is why the rate here is higher than a plain deduction
items.notes: The forfeiture risk is why this is elected carefully rather than maximised. Overestimating by $500 and losing it wipes out the saving on the first $1,600 you did spend.

items.name: Dependent care FSA — childcare paid with untaxed money
items.rateOn: up to $5,000 of childcare or eldercare costs you were going to pay anyway
items.appliesTo: employees paying for childcare or dependent care in order to work, where the employer offers the benefit. Married couples must both work, be students or be disabled to qualify at all.
items.accessNotes: Elect it at open enrollment and submit receipts as you pay. Unlike the health FSA, only money already contributed is available to reimburse, so it drains in step with payroll rather than being available up front.
requirements: $5,000 per household, not per person — $2,500 if married filing separately
Both spouses must have earned income; the exclusion is limited to the lower of the two
Care must be needed for you to work, and the provider's tax identification number must be reported
It reduces the expenses available for the separate Child and Dependent Care Credit, so you cannot claim both on the same dollars
Use-it-or-lose-it with no carryover, though a grace period is common
items.notes: Saves income tax and payroll tax on money already committed to childcare, which makes it one of the highest-certainty returns on this list for a working parent. Compare against the dependent care credit before electing — at lower incomes the credit is sometimes worth more.

items.name: Commuter benefits — pre-tax transit and parking
items.rateOn: roughly $340 a month of transit and the same again for parking
items.appliesTo: employees who commute by public transport or pay to park, at an employer offering a qualified transportation plan. Not available to the self-employed, and worth nothing if you work from home.
items.accessNotes: Elect it in the benefits portal — it is usually a monthly election you can change month to month, unlike the annual FSA lock. Transit and parking are separate limits and you can use both, so a park-and-ride commute gets roughly $680 a month of pre-tax room.
requirements: Monthly limits of roughly $340 each for transit and parking, indexed annually
Unused transit balances generally cannot be refunded in cash and are forfeited when you leave
The bicycle commuting reimbursement remains suspended and is not a route to this
The employer must run a qualified plan; there is no way to claim this on your own return
items.notes: Small, dull and completely certain: it is your marginal rate plus payroll tax on money you were already spending to get to work. The deadline is monthly, so every month you do not elect is permanently gone.

items.name: Limited-purpose FSA alongside an HSA
items.rateOn: dental and vision costs, paid pre-tax without touching HSA eligibility
items.appliesTo: people with an HSA-qualifying high-deductible plan whose employer also offers a limited-purpose FSA. Most people believe an FSA and an HSA cannot coexist, and for a general-purpose FSA that is correct.
items.accessNotes: Elect the limited-purpose version at open enrollment. It covers dental and vision only, which is precisely why it does not disqualify you from contributing to an HSA — so you can run both, protect the HSA balance for long-term compounding, and pay this year's dental bills with untaxed money.
requirements: It must be the LIMITED-PURPOSE version; a general-purpose health FSA destroys HSA eligibility for the whole year, including for your spouse
Covers dental and vision expenses, and post-deductible medical in some plan designs
Same use-it-or-lose-it rule and same roughly $3,400 limit as a general health FSA
Your employer has to offer it, and many do not
items.notes: The obscure part is that it exists at all. Used well it lets the HSA stay untouched and invested — which is the whole point of the receipt-shoebox row — while current dental and vision costs are still paid with pre-tax money.

items.name: Open enrollment — the only weeks these elections are possible
items.rateOn: the whole stack of pre-tax elections — HSA, FSA, dependent care and commuter — you can only start now
items.appliesTo: every employee with a benefits package. The dates are your employer's and typically fall between mid-October and the end of November — check your own, because this row uses the common window, not yours.
items.accessNotes: Do the whole stack in one sitting: HSA if you are on a high-deductible plan, health or limited-purpose FSA, dependent care FSA, commuter, and confirm the 401(k) deferral is at least at the full match. Outside this window most of these cannot be started or changed at all without a qualifying life event.
requirements: Missing the window generally means waiting a full year — marriage, a birth, a job change or a loss of other coverage are the usual exceptions
HSA contributions are the exception and can normally be changed any month, unlike FSA elections
Elections are per plan year, which is not always the calendar year at every employer
The cap shown is the rough sum of the FSA, dependent care and commuter limits and ignores the HSA, which has its own row
items.notes: This is the single most concentrated deadline on this list: a few weeks a year decide the entire following year's pre-tax elections, and it is the one people miss by simply not opening the email.

items.name: Chase 5/24 — the sequencing rule nobody publishes
items.rateOn: the required spending on a card bonus you can only get if you applied in the right order
items.appliesTo: people with good credit who pay their statement in full every month and are willing to track application dates. It is actively harmful to anyone who carries a balance — one month of interest at 20%+ wipes out most of a bonus.
items.accessNotes: Chase consistently declines applications from anyone who has opened five or more personal credit cards across ALL issuers in the previous twenty-four months. So Chase cards go first, before any other issuer's, if you want them at all. Business cards from most issuers do not add to the count but Chase business cards are still blocked by it.
requirements: The rule is not published by Chase anywhere; it is inferred from years of consistent, well-documented data points and could change without notice
Counts personal cards from every issuer, including authorised-user accounts in many cases
Each application is a hard credit inquiry, and new accounts lower your average account age
The bonus is taxable in some forms and not others: a sign-up bonus tied to spending is treated as a rebate, while a bonus for merely opening an account can be reported on a 1099
This only works if the required spending is spending you were going to do anyway
items.notes: The $750-on-$5,000 figure is an illustration of a typical mainstream offer at the snapshot date, not a quote — actual bonuses move constantly and are frequently targeted. The durable thing here is the CADENCE: the order you apply in decides which bonuses you can ever collect.

items.name: American Express once-per-lifetime — check before you apply
items.rateOn: the required spending on a welcome offer you only ever get one of per card
items.appliesTo: people with good credit who pay in full monthly. If you have held the specific card before, the welcome offer is usually simply unavailable and applying gains you nothing but an inquiry.
items.accessNotes: Amex terms state you may be ineligible for a welcome offer if you have or have had that card. Before applying, run the application to the point where the eligibility notice appears — it tells you, before you submit, whether you will get the bonus. That check is the entire technique.
requirements: The restriction is per specific card product, and it is stated in the offer terms rather than being folklore
Amex applies a separate limit on how many cards you may hold at once, which is not published
Referral bonuses from an existing cardholder are separate from the welcome offer and are reported as taxable income on a 1099
Retention offers on an existing card are often worth more than a new application, and cost nothing but a phone call
Only worth anything if you clear the statement every month
items.notes: The illustrative bonus figure is a typical mainstream offer at the snapshot date and will not match what you are shown; the eligibility check before submitting is the part that is always true and always worth doing.

items.name: ESPP — the 15% discount, and the lookback that doubles it
items.rateOn: every dollar you put through the plan
items.termLabel: Money is held until the purchase date
items.appliesTo: employees at companies that run a Section 423 employee stock purchase plan, which is common at public companies and rare elsewhere
items.accessNotes: Enrol through your equity or payroll portal during the enrolment window — most plans open twice a year and will not let you join in between. Set a contribution percentage; payroll withholds it and buys shares on the purchase date. Selling immediately captures the discount and avoids holding a concentrated position in the company that also pays your salary.
requirements: Employer runs a Section 423 ESPP
Enrolment window is open
Payroll deduction for the offering period
items.notes: A 15% discount is not a 15% return: you pay 85 cents for a dollar, which is a 17.6% gain the moment the shares land. Because the money goes in over a six-month offering period rather than all at once, the annualised figure on the average balance is roughly double that again. A lookback provision — where the price is the LOWER of the offering-date and purchase-date price — makes it larger still in a rising market, and never smaller. This is the highest guaranteed return available to most employees who have one, and the reason it goes unclaimed is that nobody tells you it exists. Selling on the purchase date makes the discount ordinary income and is a disqualifying disposition; holding longer can convert part of the gain to long-term rates and also exposes you to the share price. The discount is the certain part.

items.name: ESPP without a lookback — still a discount worth taking
items.rateOn: every dollar you put through the plan
items.termLabel: Money is held until the purchase date
items.appliesTo: employees whose plan offers a smaller discount, commonly 5%, with no lookback provision
items.accessNotes: Same enrolment mechanics as any ESPP. Read the plan document for two numbers: the discount percentage and whether there is a lookback. Both are in the summary plan description.
requirements: Employer runs an ESPP
Enrolment window is open
items.notes: A 5% discount is a 5.3% gain on the money, which sounds small and is not: the money is only committed for the offering period, so the annualised figure is far higher, and the outcome does not depend on the share price if you sell on the purchase date. Worth checking the plan document rather than assuming — plans differ, and a 5% no-lookback plan and a 15% lookback plan are described identically in most benefits summaries.

items.name: The wash-sale rule — the 30 days that decide whether a harvested loss counts
items.rateOn: a harvested loss that would otherwise be disallowed
items.appliesTo: anyone harvesting losses in a taxable account, which is most people who hold funds outside a retirement plan
items.accessNotes: After selling at a loss, do not buy the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days either side — and that includes purchases in your IRA and, in practice, automatic dividend reinvestment you forgot was switched on. Buying a different fund tracking a different index is the standard way to stay invested without triggering it.
requirements: A realised loss in a taxable account
No repurchase within the 61-day window
items.notes: This row is worth exactly as much as the loss it protects, which is why it has no rate of its own. The commonest way people lose a harvest is not a deliberate repurchase but an automatic one: reinvested dividends inside the 30-day window disallow a proportional part of the loss, and nothing warns you. The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares rather than destroyed, so it is deferred rather than lost — but deferred to a year you did not choose.
items.uncappedNote: There is no cap because this is not a contribution — it is a rule about timing. It is worth exactly as much as the loss it stops you forfeiting, which depends entirely on how large that loss was.

items.name: Asset location — the same portfolio, taxed less
items.rateOn: the tax-inefficient part of a portfolio held in the wrong account
items.appliesTo: anyone holding both a taxable account and a tax-advantaged one, with a mix of bonds and equities across them
items.accessNotes: Hold the things that throw off ordinary income — bond funds, REITs, high-turnover strategies — inside the IRA or 401(k), and hold broad equity index funds in the taxable account where their gains are unrealised and their dividends are qualified. Rearranging inside a retirement account triggers no tax at all, so most of this can be done in an afternoon with no consequences.
requirements: Both a taxable and a tax-advantaged account
Assets that differ in tax efficiency
items.notes: The same holdings in the same proportions, sorted differently between accounts, and the difference is a persistent drag avoided every year rather than a one-off. It is worth most when a large bond allocation sits in a taxable account throwing off ordinary income taxed at your top rate. It is worth nothing if all your money is in one account type, and this app cannot tell which case you are in — the figure here is the tax on a typical bond yield, not a promise.
items.uncappedNote: No cap, because nothing is being contributed: the same money is simply held in a different account. The value scales with how much tax-inefficient holding you have in the wrong place.

items.name: SEP IRA — a fifth of self-employment income, deductible
items.rateOn: money contributed from self-employment income
items.earlyExitPenalty: 10% early-distribution penalty plus ordinary income tax before 59½
items.appliesTo: anyone with self-employment or freelance income, including a side business alongside a normal job
items.accessNotes: Open one at any major custodian in about ten minutes. The contribution is deductible against self-employment income and can be made right up to the tax filing deadline including extensions, which makes it the rare deduction still available after the year has ended.
requirements: Self-employment income
An account opened before the filing deadline
items.notes: Roughly a fifth of net self-employment earnings, deductible, with far less paperwork than a solo 401(k) — no plan document, no annual filing at small balances. A solo 401(k) usually allows a larger contribution at modest income because of its employee deferral, so compare the two before choosing. The deadline flexibility is the real advantage: it is one of the very few moves that still works in April for the year that has already finished.

items.name: HSA catch-up at 55 — an extra $1,000 of triple-tax space
items.rateOn: the additional catch-up contribution
items.appliesTo: anyone aged 55 or over with a qualifying high-deductible health plan
items.accessNotes: Add it to your existing HSA contribution — no separate account and no extra form. If both spouses are 55 or over, each catch-up needs its own HSA in that spouse's name, which is the part people miss and cannot fix retroactively.
requirements: Age 55 or over
Enrolled in a qualifying high-deductible health plan
items.notes: The HSA is the only account that is deductible going in, untaxed while it grows, and untaxed coming out for medical costs. The catch-up adds a further slice of that space every year from 55, and unlike the 401(k) catch-up almost nobody uses it. The two-spouse detail matters: a married couple can make two catch-up contributions only if there are two HSAs, and opening the second one in December does not recover the years it did not exist.

items.name: Student loan interest — deductible without itemising
items.rateOn: up to $2,500 of interest paid in the year
items.appliesTo: anyone paying interest on a qualified student loan, subject to an income phase-out
items.accessNotes: Your servicer issues a 1098-E. It is an above-the-line deduction, so it works whether or not you itemise — which is why it is missed by people who take the standard deduction and assume no deductions apply to them.
requirements: Qualified student loan interest paid
Income below the phase-out
Not filing separately
items.notes: Small in absolute terms and almost free to claim, which is a combination that makes it worth listing. It phases out over an income range and disappears entirely for married filing separately. If somebody else can claim you as a dependent, you cannot take it.

items.name: I-bond timing — a purchase on the 30th earns the whole month
items.rateOn: a purchase made near the end of a month rather than the start of the next
items.termLabel: Twelve months minimum, three months of interest forfeited before five years
items.appliesTo: anyone buying savings bonds at TreasuryDirect
items.accessNotes: Savings bonds are dated to the first of the month in which you buy them, so a purchase settled on the 30th earns that entire month's interest. Leave a couple of business days: TreasuryDirect settles on its own schedule and a purchase started on the 31st can land in the following month.
requirements: A TreasuryDirect account
Purchase settled before month end
items.notes: A small, certain, purely mechanical edge — close to a free extra month of interest for choosing one date over another a few days later. The figure here is the value of that month at recent composite rates, not a yield on the bond itself. It is listed because it is exactly the kind of thing that is obvious once known and invisible until then.
